title: The Edge of Winter
subtitle: Conclusion of Phase IV and the German military situation before the renewed offensive towards Moscow.
author: Robert M. Dobo
summary: The Orsha conference exposes German depletion, yet another offensive is prepared while Soviet defence and mobilisation continue.
body:
The day before another attempt

On 13 November, German chiefs of staff met at Orsha to discuss how much more their armies could accomplish. The figures before them described a force seriously diminished by five months of war. The next day, Army Group Centre was still preparing another attempt against Moscow, while Soviet Forty-Ninth Army attacked near Serpukhov. The phase closes at this conjunction: German leaders had acknowledged the limits of their means but continued to demand an offensive, and Soviet commanders were doing more than waiting for it. The renewed German attacks would begin on the northern wing on 15 November, with the major mobile thrusts following on subsequent days. [1][2]

Six weeks earlier, Typhoon had begun with the prospect of destroying the armies defending Moscow before a prolonged campaign became necessary. The Vyazma and Bryansk encirclements inflicted the expected catastrophe, but the expected end of resistance did not follow. Soviet forces rebuilt the approaches, government institutions survived the evacuation crisis and Tula remained defended. The question facing Germany had consequently changed. It was no longer whether a major Soviet defeat could be achieved; October had answered that. It was whether the depleted attacking force could now secure a strategic result that its earlier victory had failed to deliver. [1][2]

At Orsha, Franz Halder, chief of the army general staff, accepted that the original objectives could no longer be achieved in full. He nevertheless argued that the army must inflict as much damage as possible before the end of the year because Soviet recovery would make the following campaign harder. The argument turned exhaustion into a reason to continue: stopping allowed the enemy to rebuild, but continuing would consume more of Germany's remaining strength. The chiefs of staff responded with evidence of what their commands could actually support. Their disagreement concerned the balance between those risks, not the existence of a fresh army waiting to be committed. [1]

Three army groups, three problems

Army Group North still held Tikhvin, taken on 8 November, but possession of the rail junction had not delivered Leeb's full objective. Soviet forces were contesting the German salient, and the hoped-for link with Finnish forces near the Svir had not been made. The railway towards Ladoga remained cut while the town was German-held, so Leningrad's supply crisis persisted. But Leeb needed troops both to defend the salient and to maintain the broader siege line. The U.S. Army history reports that by this stage he had exhausted his reserves reaching Tikhvin. A commander can win a local objective and still be unable to turn it into the next strategic step.[1][3][4]

The Soviet response was developing on different parts of the salient. Fifty-Second Army had attacked near Malaya Vishera on 12 November, while Fourth Army's larger assault on Tikhvin still lay ahead. Fifty-Fourth Army held its own responsibilities nearer the Volkhov. These separate efforts required Leeb to consider more than the defence of the captured junction. Pressure on an approach or flank could force him to commit troops needed elsewhere, even before it produced a breakthrough. On 14 November, the German salient remained in place, but Soviet action was beginning to test the connections on which its continued possession depended. [5][6]

Army Group Centre had the most politically charged objective. Bock's forces faced Moscow from a broad arc. Ninth Army held the north near Kalinin; Third Panzer Group stood west of Klin; Fourth Panzer Group and Fourth Army occupied the central approaches; Second Panzer Army faced Tula and the Oka from the south. Second Army covered the vulnerable far southern flank east of Orel and Kursk. This deployment was not a neat ring already closed around the capital. The north and south arms had separate routes and substantial Soviet forces between them and their projected meeting places. Tula remained Soviet-held, making it a live obstacle on the southern side.[2][7][1]

Army Group South remained spread between eastern Ukraine and Crimea. First Panzer Army was moving towards Rostov; Seventeenth Army operated along the Donets; Sixth Army had not resumed the further advance sought by its superiors. In Crimea, Eleventh Army had penetrated the peninsula but still faced Sevastopol. The account of the Orsha report described the Kerch area as almost cleared, indicating an operation still in progress rather than a completed conquest. These situations gave Rundstedt no single, finished southern victory from which to draw a free reserve. Each army had acquired further demands through its advance, and their prospects depended on different routes, opponents and remaining strengths. [7][8]

A prospective line

Halder discussed lines beyond the positions the armies held, including objectives east of Moscow. These were prospective limits for further operations, not a record of German control on 14 November. The conference's importance lies in the distance between such ambitions and the force available to pursue them. [1]

What Orsha revealed

The 13 November Orsha meeting is unusually useful because it brings the German command's aspirations and its internal accounting into the same room. The U.S. Army history reports staff figures of roughly 686,000 German casualties by 1 November, one third of the eastern front's motor vehicles worn out or beyond repair, and panzer divisions with about thirty-five percent of their original tank strength. These are German staff estimates transmitted through a later history; they are not a count of men or vehicles standing at each location on 14 November. Their significance is that senior officers knew the combat system had been severely diminished before they asked it to move again.[1]

The figures described several different kinds of depletion. The casualty total included more than deaths; it measured personnel removed by the campaign. Vehicle and tank figures concerned equipment condition and availability, while the conversion of 136 divisions into an estimated equivalent of eighty-three full-strength formations was a staff judgment about effective power. These measures cannot be added together, but they point in the same direction. The order of battle retained the names of a large army while many of its formations had lost a substantial part of the strength with which they began. Planning on the basis of intact divisional titles would therefore exaggerate what commanders could concentrate. [1][7]

Halder's initial proposals still reached well beyond the immediate front. Even the more limited line envisaged positions east of Moscow, while northern operations were to seek a connection towards the Svir. The larger ambitions included cities and resource areas far beyond what the armies could presently support. These proposals reveal the persistence of the campaign's original logic: continued movement was expected to deny the Soviet Union the means to recover. The difficulty was that the movement required more strength than the current force possessed. Orsha brought that contradiction into the command discussion through the testimony of the officers responsible for each army group's operations. [1]

The responses were concrete. Army Group North's chief of staff, Kurt Brennecke, said Leeb had no divisions available for a further drive east unless forces were first released from the fighting west of Leningrad. Army Group South's Georg von Sodenstern reported Rundstedt's concern that a march to Maikop would exhaust First Panzer Army for much of the following year. Bock's chief of staff, Hans von Greiffenberg, resisted a suggestion to delay the Moscow operation for roughly two weeks in the hope of assembling a deeper thrust. Each response identified a different limit. The army groups were being asked to produce another strategic result from forces already committed to unfinished tasks. [1]

Halder reduced his immediate ambitions after hearing these objections, but he did not abandon further operations. He expected the army groups to obtain as much as they could from their troops until about mid-December. Moscow was still to face stronger pressure, Army Group North was to continue around Tikhvin and Leningrad, and the southern advance was to go on within narrower limits. More distant objectives were deferred. The conclusion was therefore a contraction of aims rather than a clear termination of the offensive campaign. The chiefs had demonstrated that the original programme was beyond their means; the leadership still required additional gains before accepting the consequences of a longer war. [1]

The implications of a prolonged war had reached beyond field headquarters. The German planning history records General Friedrich Fromm, head of the Replacement Army, urging that an attempt be made to reach peace while the army could still fight to a draw. Halder rejected the proposal. This was a suggestion inside the German command, not a peace offer transmitted to the Soviet government, and it did not become policy. Its significance is that continued attack was not the only possibility raised by officers assessing the situation. The leadership chose to seek further military gains despite arguments that the campaign had already exhausted the basis for its intended decision.

The choice also complicates later efforts to attribute the continuation of the offensive to one man's will. The record shows disagreement among commanders and a general staff still seeking damage to the enemy before Soviet recovery strengthened it. Halder's narrowed programme preserved that purpose even after more distant objectives were deferred. The decision to continue emerged from an institution confronting the failure of its assumptions, rather than from ignorance of the losses already suffered. [7][1]

Moscow's defenders

The Soviet command had also altered its structure as the front stabilised. Zhukov's Western Front covered the direct approaches, while Konev's Kalinin Front protected the northern side. On 10 November, Zhukov took over Fiftieth Army as Bryansk Front was being deactivated, bringing the Tula defence into his responsibility. The later transfer of Thirtieth Army from Kalinin Front had not yet occurred on the fourteenth. The distinction matters because coordination was changing during the interval before the German attack. The capital's defence was becoming more integrated, but its final mid-November command arrangement should not be projected backwards onto every preceding day. [2]

Moscow itself had experienced evacuation, public alarm and emergency rule in October, yet it remained a functioning military and political centre. On 7 November Stalin reviewed a parade in Red Square and spoke to soldiers. His parade address invoked Russian military figures; in his speech the previous evening he had stressed the coalition with Britain and the United States. It would be wrong to let the image of the parade stand for an army already secure. A public ceremony could reassure residents and signal continuity while the front remained uncertain. It also sent troops towards combat. The ceremony belongs in the story because political authority and morale mattered to a capital under threat, but it could not substitute for guns on the western roads.[1][2]

The Anglo-American connection had also become more concrete since the October supply conference. In his 4 November reply to Roosevelt, Stalin accepted the proposed billion-dollar arrangement and its delayed, interest-free repayment terms. He also offered Soviet commodities needed by the United States and welcomed direct communication between the two leaders. The exchange reveals a relationship being built through reciprocal undertakings rather than a sudden erasure of political distrust. Its timing mattered: Moscow could present the commitment as evidence that continued resistance had powerful external support. Its battlefield effects still depended on ships, ports, railway wagons and allocation decisions. An agreement concluded in the Kremlin could strengthen the prospect of sustaining the war without immediately supplying a tank brigade west of Moscow.[9][10]

On the ground, Tula remained the southern hinge. Soviet Fiftieth Army and local defenders held the industrial city despite German pressure. Guderian could seek a way around it, but the city could threaten movement and supply along the flank of a projected southern envelopment. In the north, German Third and Fourth Panzer Groups could plan routes towards Klin and the Moscow–Volga Canal, but Soviet positions and the distance between spearheads remained real obstacles. Zhukov's job was to keep these approaches connected as a defensive system, not merely to hold an imaginary circle at the capital's edge. The result on 14 November remained undecided.[2][7]

The Soviet counterblow near Serpukhov on 14 November captures that uncertainty. According to the U.S. Army history, Forty-Ninth Army, reinforced with cavalry, rifle and tank elements, attacked the right flank of German Fourth Army in the Serpukhov sector. Zhukov was reluctant about such “counterblows” because he expected the main German attack and doubted the value of spending forces in a limited blow. Stalin pressed for them. This was neither the great December counteroffensive nor a proof that Soviet initiative had decisively passed to every front. It was a contested command decision within an active defence.[2]

Zhukov later described the counterblows as Stalin's demand and judged them likely to complicate the defence. The U.S. Army account uses that recollection alongside its operational reconstruction. The distinction between the dated attack and the commander's later explanation matters: Forty-Ninth Army's action on 14 November is the event, while Zhukov's assessment is evidence of a disagreement about its wisdom. The dispute exposes a real operational choice. Attacking might disrupt German preparations, but it also committed formations that could be needed to meet the expected assault. Soviet leaders did not enter the next battle with a single uncontested understanding of how best to defend Moscow. [2]

Bock's own instructions also contained unresolved tension. He retained ambitious routes around and beyond Moscow while telling Halder and his army commanders that he doubted the army group could advance much beyond the canal north of the capital and the Moscow River to the south. The U.S. Army history records Third Panzer Group's resulting complaint that its mission was unclear. This was a command problem in addition to a supply problem. Subordinate formations needed to know whether they were preparing a close encirclement or a much deeper movement, because the force, fuel and flank protection required were different. Uncertainty at the top persisted as the attack approached. [2]

The offensive's date

A Soviet Forty-Ninth Army counterblow in the Serpukhov sector began on 14 November. The main renewed German attack towards Moscow opened on subsequent days, beginning on the northern wing on 15 November. The two movements should not be combined into a single “14 November German offensive” on the map.[2][7]

Roads, weather and repair

The approach of freezing weather made the German decision more tempting. Hardening ground could let armoured units move beyond roads where autumn mud had confined them. It did not replenish tank strength or repair a worn engine. Short days limited flying time; low cloud could obstruct air support. A front prepared to exploit a temporary improvement in mobility still needed fuel at the right place and infantry able to follow. The army's supply chain had to convert or repair railway track, transport loads beyond the railhead and distribute them along a broad arc. Each additional mile east increased demand on vehicles already worn by months of war.[2][7][1]

The staff debate about winter clothing is often compressed into the statement that Germany had none. The evidence is more precise and more revealing: material existed in rear storage but could not be brought forward in sufficient volume without displacing other urgent traffic. A frontline soldier's exposure therefore resulted from planning assumptions and a transport allocation, not from a mysterious inability to manufacture a coat. The Russian winter had been foreseeable as a season; what the German high command had not built was a supply system prepared to sustain this invasion through it. The consequence was felt unevenly by men whose unit, road and depot positions differed.[1][7]

Soviet reinforcement had improved the defence without eliminating its unevenness. Some formations were experienced; others had been assembled quickly and still lacked training. Zhukov had to incorporate them into sectors whose responsibilities were changing, while the Stavka retained forces for further use. The German command could therefore face determined resistance from particular units without confronting an opponent of uniform quality along the whole line. Equally, Soviet weaknesses did not establish that another defeat would exhaust the state's remaining capacity. October had already shown the danger of that inference. The coming operation would test the forces actually available, not an abstract image of inexhaustible Soviet manpower. [2]

The railway figures discussed at Orsha explain why stocks in the rear were not the same as support at the front. The German account records only about 500 captured Soviet locomotives and 21,000 wagons across the occupied territory, roughly a tenth of the stated requirement. German rolling stock needed converted track; compatible equipment alone did not solve damage, distance or competing demands. The same limited capacity had to carry ammunition, food, fuel and winter clothing. Leaving clothing in storage was therefore a decision within a strained distribution system, with direct consequences for the troops expected to continue fighting. The difficulty was known before the renewed attack began. [1]

Civilians and occupation

In Leningrad, the narrowing margin of survival could be measured in bread. On 13 November, daily entitlements fell to 300 grams for ordinary workers and 150 grams for office workers, dependants and children under twelve, as Nicolas Werth's historical introduction records. These were ration entitlements, not a guarantee of adequate nourishment. The more familiar minimum of 125 grams belonged to the further reduction on 20 November, beyond this phase. Tikhvin's loss intensified a supply crisis already in progress; it did not begin the hunger or make the later ration valid on an earlier date. [11]

Across occupied territory, the invasion's violence continued after battles moved elsewhere. Soviet prisoners remained under a German system of deliberate deprivation, exposure and killing. Jewish communities faced persecution and murder by security units, police, military formations and collaborating forces, with participation established through particular institutions and acts. The army's growing operational difficulties did not suspend these policies. In some cases, as Reichenau's October order showed, commanders explicitly used their conception of the campaign to justify excluding civilians and prisoners from assistance. Military exhaustion and criminal policy belonged to the same war, but they were not interchangeable explanations of the deaths behind the front. [12][13]

The contrast between Moscow and Leningrad remained stark. Moscow was threatened but connected to the Soviet rear; Leningrad was already enduring a blockade whose supply route had suffered another blow. German instructions envisaged denying sustenance and refuge to Moscow's population if the planned operation succeeded. In Leningrad, isolation was already producing deprivation. Keeping intention and implementation separate does not diminish the responsibility involved in either. It identifies what people faced at the phase's endpoint: a threatened policy in one capital of Soviet political and industrial life, and an existing siege in another. [7][14][3]

The Soviet state's survival also imposed burdens that a narrative of successful resistance must retain. Emergency powers in Moscow included summary force; the security apparatus screened and punished soldiers after retreat; industrial removal disrupted production and displaced workers. These measures did not have one purpose or one moral character. Evacuation could preserve livelihoods and future production while exposing people to hardship; a criminal order to kill selected civilians pursued a different end. The phase's history requires those distinctions because the people subjected to state power experienced particular decisions, not an undifferentiated contest between two national populations. [15][16][17]

Where Phase IV ends

Germany retained the capacity to attack on 14 November. Army Group Centre was preparing renewed operations, First Panzer Army still threatened Rostov, and Army Group North held Tikhvin. Yet these positions no longer supported the expectation of a short, completed campaign. Soviet armies continued to fight, the state continued to mobilise and the German command had acknowledged that its remaining strength could not fulfil the programme imagined earlier in the year. The military initiative had survived; the original relationship between initiative and decisive victory had not. Another offensive was becoming a means of postponing the strategic consequences of that failure. [2][5][7]

The phase's central development was therefore the separation of German battlefield success from its expected political result. Typhoon destroyed the Soviet front it first attacked, but a new defence formed behind the disaster. Occupation deprived the Soviet state of cities and resources, but evacuation and production farther east preserved part of its capacity to continue. The response was costly, uneven and coercive; it was also effective enough to prevent Germany's victories from ending the war. None of this made Soviet victory inevitable in November. It meant that Germany would have to keep fighting an opponent its autumn offensive had been intended to eliminate as an organised military power. [1][2][3]

The decision to attack again followed from that unresolved result. Halder feared the consequences of allowing Soviet recovery, while the field commands reported that their own means were deteriorating. Bock retained ambitious instructions despite doubts about how far his forces could go. On the other side, Zhukov was preparing to receive the blow while contesting Stalin's demand for counterattacks. The phase ends with decisions still being made under uncertainty, but that uncertainty had a changed foundation. Both commands were now preparing for further battle after the failure of Germany's attempt to turn the October catastrophe into a final decision. [2][1]

The opening attacks had promised a conclusion before winter. By 14 November, German leaders were discussing how much more their soldiers could accomplish before exhaustion and the season imposed another limit. Soviet defenders had preserved Moscow and Tula, but millions of people remained under occupation, prisoners faced lethal captivity, and Leningrad's inhabitants received reduced bread rations. Survival at the level of the state had not ended the danger to those people. The next offensive would begin from this altered situation: Germany still able to inflict immense harm, the Soviet Union still able to resist, and the decisive end sought in September farther from achievement than the October victories had suggested. [1][2][12][11]

sourceMethod: Numbered notes link claims to the consulted passages. The Orsha figures are reported contemporary staff assessments, with casualties, vehicle condition and divisional equivalents kept distinct. Zhukov’s interpretation of the counterblows is retrospective. Bread entitlements are checked in Nicolas Werth’s published introduction; later November reductions are explicitly outside the phase. This is a local prose revision; maps and their separately stored Study Context passages have not been revised.
